props.title: My Name Is Khan
props.initialSlug: A Muslim man's journey to prove "I'm not a terrorist"

sections.content: My Name Is Khan marked a pivotal moment in Bollywood's approach to both post-9/11 narratives and neurodivergent representation. Shah Rukh Khan's portrayal of Rizwan Khan, a Muslim man with Asperger's syndrome navigating post-9/11 America, builds on the emotional depth seen in Rain Man (1988) while adding crucial cultural dimensions. The film's unflinching look at Islamophobia parallels themes explored in The Visitor (2007), but through a distinctly South Asian lens.

sections.content: Director Karan Johar deliberately breaks from his signature glossy romance style seen in Kuch Kuch Hota Hai (1998) to craft a more grounded narrative. The film's cross-country journey structure echoes Forrest Gump (1994), but uses this framework to expose various facets of post-9/11 American society. The hurricane sequence, while melodramatic, draws powerful parallels to actual media coverage of Hurricane Katrina and its disproportionate impact on minority communities.

The film's portrayal of an interfaith relationship between Khan and Mandira (Kajol) builds on earlier Bollywood examinations of Hindu-Muslim relations like Bombay (1995), but places it within a contemporary global context. The personal becomes political as their domestic life intersects with larger societal tensions, similar to the approach taken in American Son (2019). SUBHEAD: Breaking Bollywood Conventions

sections.content: While maintaining some Bollywood elements like elaborate musical numbers, My Name Is Khan significantly departs from commercial Indian cinema's typical three-act structure. The film's treatment of autism avoids both Hollywood's savant stereotypes and Bollywood's tendency toward broad characterizations. Instead, it draws influence from international films like The Black Balloon (2008) and Adam (2009) in its nuanced portrayal of neurodivergent experiences.
